paragraphs.text: Preface

1. For those men who set out from their own country and meet with contests and dangers beyond its borders, if some reverse befalls them by land or by sea, there remains to the survivors their own land and city and homeland, so that they would not all be utterly destroyed.

2. But for those who are about to face danger for the greatest of things—their temples, their homeland, their parents, their children, and all the rest—the contest is not equal nor alike; rather, for those who are saved and have defended themselves well, it means that they will be formidable to their enemies and hard to attack for the rest of time, while for those who have borne themselves badly in the dangers, no hope of safety will remain.

3. Those, therefore, who are about to contend for things so many and so great must be deficient in no preparation and no zeal, but must take forethought for many works of every kind, so that through no fault of their own may they be seen to have failed.

4. But if after all some misfortune does occur, at least the survivors might one day restore their fortunes to their former state, just as some of the Greeks, having come to the very brink of ruin, yet recovered themselves.
Chapter 1

1. We must, then, consider the marshalling of the men in relation to the size of the city, the layout of the town, the posting of the guards and their rounds, and all the other duties for which men are needed throughout the city, and make our divisions accordingly.

2. Those who go out on campaign must be organized with a view to the places along their route—how they ought to march past dangerous, fortified, narrow, level, commanding, and ambush-prone ground, and the crossings of rivers, and the deployments arising from such places.
3. But those who keep the walls and guard the city need no such organization, only one suited to the places within the city and to the present danger.
4. First, then, one must assign the most prudent men, those most experienced in war, who shall be about the magistrates.

5. Then, for the rest, one must pick out the men most capable of hard work, and, dividing them, form them into companies, so that they may be available, ready stationed and able to serve, for the sorties and the rounds throughout the city and the relief of hard-pressed posts, or for any other like service.

6. They must be loyal and content with the established order; for such a body, kept together, is a great safeguard against the plots of others, serving as a citadel, and would be a terror to those in the city who wish to act against it.
7. Let their leader and overseer be a man prudent in all other respects and vigorous, and one to whom the greatest dangers would come if a revolution should occur.

8. Of the remainder, one should select the most robust in age and youth and post them to the guard-duties and the walls, and distribute the surplus multitude in proportion to the length of the nights and the number of the watches.

9. As for the crowds, one should assign some to the market-place, some to the theatre, and the rest to the other open spaces in the city, so that, as far as possible, no part of the city be left empty.
Chapter 2

1. It is best to blind the useless open spaces in the city—so that men need not be stationed in them—by trenching them and making them as impassable as possible for those who wish to start a revolt and to seize them beforehand.

2. The Lacedaemonians, indeed, when the Thebans invaded, pulling down material from the nearest houses and from the field-walls and party-walls, and filling baskets with earth and stones in different places, one party here and another there—and they say they used also the bronze tripods from the temples, of which there were many and large ones—and, blocking up with these too beforehand the entrances and passages and open spaces of the town, prevented those who attempted to break in from reaching the town itself.

3. The Plataeans, when they perceived by night that the Thebans were in the city, observing that these were not many nor engaged in the work that was fitting, but supposing, for all that, that they held the city, judged that by attacking them they would easily prevail. They therefore at once devised the following stratagem.

4. Some of the magistrates made agreements with the Thebans in the market-place, while others secretly passed word to the rest of the citizens not to come out of their houses scattered, but, one and two at a time, to dig through the party-walls and gather together secretly at one another's houses.

5. When a force large enough to fight had been made ready, they blocked the passages and lanes with wagons without their draught-animals, and at a signal, having assembled, they rushed upon the Thebans.

6. At the same time the women and the household slaves were on the roofs, so that, when the Thebans wished to act and to defend themselves in the dark, the harm done by the wagons was no less than that done by the men set upon them. For the one party fled, not knowing the way to safety because of the barricades of wagons, while the others, pursuing with knowledge of the ground, quickly destroyed many.

7. One must, however, set down also the considerations opposite to these: that, if there is but a single open space, there is danger to those in the city, should the plotters seize it beforehand; for, the place being common and single, the work would belong to those who acted first. But if there are two or three such places, the following advantages would result.

8. If they seize one or two places, the remaining one would be left to their opponents; and if they seize all, then, being divided and dispersed, they would be in a weaker position against their opponents who are concentrated, unless they should outnumber those in the city in each detachment. And in the same way, in all other matters too, one must take into account the considerations opposite to those set down above, that one may not heedlessly adopt some other course.
Chapter 3

1. When a fresh fear comes upon a city that is unorganized, one might most quickly set the citizens in order for the guarding of the city if one were to assign by lot to each tribe some part of the wall, to which the tribes will come at once and stand guard. Let them guard a stretch of wall proportioned to the numbers of each tribe.
2. Then, in this way, one should pick out from each tribe those able to do bodily work for the market-place and the rounds, and for whatever other service such men are needed.

3. In like manner, too, when a fortress is garrisoned by allies, let some part of the wall be assigned to each of the allied contingents to guard. And if the citizens are in mutual suspicion, one must station trustworthy men at each ascent of the wall, who will be there to prevent it, should anyone else attempt to climb up.

4. In peacetime the citizens should be organized in the following way as well. First, appoint for each lane a lane-warden, the most reasonable and prudent man, to whom they will gather if anything unexpected happens by night.

5. The lane-wardens should lead the lanes nearest the market-place into the market-place, those nearest the theatre into the theatre, and to the other open spaces let each gather those nearest, together with the men who have brought their arms to them.

6. For thus they would most quickly reach their proper places and be nearest their own homes, and could, while managing their affairs, send word to their households—children and wives—since they would remain not far from them. And the magistrates must have been assigned beforehand by lot the place to which each is to go and from which he will dispatch some of those assembled to the parapets; and they will be leaders to care for the rest, provided they take the lead from the start in the following way.
Chapter 4

1. They must at once have arranged for themselves signals by which they will not fail to recognize those who approach them. For something of this kind has already happened. Chalcis on the Euripus was captured by an exile setting out from Eretria, one of the men in the city having contrived the following.

2. In the most deserted part of the city, where there were gates that were not opened, he kept a tower-chamber, and while guarding it by day and night, he secretly by night burned through the bar and there admitted soldiers.

3. When about two thousand men had gathered in the market-place, the alarm for battle was sounded in haste. Many of the Chalcidians perished through ignorance; for in their terror they brought and laid down their arms before the enemy as if before friends, each man supposing that he himself was the last to arrive.
4. Thus most of them perished one and two at a time, until some time later they realized what was happening, the city being already in enemy hands.

5. When at war, therefore, and especially when the enemy are near, one must first see that whatever is sent out from the city by land or by sea on any errand is sent to those who remain behind with signals, both for day and for night, so that they may not be in doubt, when men appear, whether they are friends or enemies.

6. And when men have gone out on some errand, one should also send others to find out the result, so that those who remain may learn of such matters as far in advance as possible; for it would greatly help, with a view to the future, to prepare from a longer way off.
7. To those who do not act thus, what has befallen will be made plain by certain things that have already happened, which I cite as a clear example and testimony.

8. For it was reported to Pisistratus, while he was general of the Athenians, that the men of Megara, arriving in boats, were attempting to attack by night the women of the Athenians who were celebrating the Thesmophoria at Eleusis. Pisistratus, hearing this, laid an ambush beforehand.

9. And when the men from Megara, supposing themselves undetected, had disembarked and gone some distance from the sea, Pisistratus rose up from the ambush, overcame the men, and destroyed most of them, and became master of the boats in which they had come.
10. Then at once, having manned the boats with his own soldiers, he took those of the women most suited to sail along, and put in to Megara, late, at some distance from the city.

11. Seeing the boats sailing in, many of the Megarians came down to meet them—the boards of magistrates and the rest—to look on, supposing, as was natural, that as many captive women as possible were being brought in . . . and the men, disembarking with daggers, struck down some, and seized into the boats as many of the most prominent as they could.
12. And so it was done. It is clear, then, that gatherings and dispatches must be made with signals, and with the men not failing to recognize one another.
Chapter 5

1. Next, the gatekeepers should be appointed not at random but men prudent and shrewd, and indeed able always to be suspicious of something being brought in; and besides, men of property, those who have pledges in the city—I mean children and a wife—and not such as might, through want, or the pressure of debts, or some other difficulty, be persuaded by certain people, or might themselves urge others on toward revolution.
2. Leucon, the tyrant of the Bosporus, used to dismiss from their pay even those of the garrison who were debtors through dicing or other forms of dissipation.
Chapter 6

1. One must also station day-watchmen before the city, on high ground visible from as far off as possible; and let at least three keep watch at each post, not men taken at random but experienced in war, so that the watchman may not, through ignorance, by his own conjecture, signal or report something into the city and trouble the people to no purpose.
2. The inexperienced in formations and war suffer this, being ignorant of the enemy's operations and movements—whether they are done by design or by chance.
3. But the experienced man, recognizing the enemy's preparation and numbers and marches and the rest of the army's movement, will thus make plain the truth.
4. If there are no such places from which the signals are visible to the city, there should be relays at one place after another to take up the raised signals, who will signal them into the city.

5. The day-watchmen should also be swift of foot, so that, when something cannot be made plain through signals but one of them must of necessity report it, they may be able to arrive quickly and report from as far off as possible.

6. It is best, when the ground is suitable for horses and horses are available, to set horsemen in a chain, so that reports may come more quickly by them. The day-watchmen should be sent out from the city at dawn or while it is still night, so that they may not be plainly seen by the enemy's scouts as they go to their watch-posts by day.

7. Let them not have one and the same watchword . . . , so that neither willingly nor unwillingly, should they be captured by the enemy, may they be able to tell the watchword of those in the city. And the day-watchmen should be ordered to raise their signals from time to time, just as the fire-signallers raise their beacons.
Chapter 7
1. When the land is rich in crops and the enemy are not far off, it is likely that many of those in the city will be spending their time about the nearby fields, eager for the harvest.

2. These, then, must be gathered into the city in the following way. First, give the signal to those outside, at sunset, to come back to the city; and if they are scattered over a still wider area of the countryside, let the signal be relayed, so that all, or most, may come into the city.

3. When the signal to come in has been given to these, the signal is then given to those in the city to take their evening meal; and the third signal is for them to go to their guard and take up their posts.

4. How this should be done, and how the beacons should be raised, has been told more fully in the book on Preparation, whence the instruction must be taken, so that I may not happen to write twice about the same things.
Chapter 8

1. After this, when expecting a larger and greater enemy force into the country, one must first make the country hard for the enemy to attack, hard to camp in, hard to draw supplies from, and the rivers hard to cross and more numerous.

2. As for the enemy's landings, what sorts of contrivances and snares should be prepared for those disembarking on the sandy and firm shores, and what sorts of barriers should be prepared at the harbours of the country and the city, against ships sailing in, or so that ships that have sailed in cannot sail out;
3. and the things deliberately left behind in the country, but which would be of use to the enemy—for wall-building, say, or tent-making, or some other purpose—

4. how one must make them useless, or, without destroying them, hide away the food and drink and the ripe produce in the fields and the rest throughout the country, and how one must make the standing waters undrinkable, and the horse-country unfit for horses—

5. concerning all these matters, how each of them should be done is for the present passed over here, that the work be not, on this point too, made excessively long; but it has been fully written about in the book on Preparation.
Chapter 9

1. If those advancing against you attempt to grow over-bold, this is what should be done. First, one must occupy with men certain positions of one's own country; then, calling an assembly of one's own soldiers or citizens, announce to them, among other things, that they have some operation in hand against the enemy, and that, whenever the trumpet sounds by night, those of military age are to be ready, take up their arms, gather at an appointed place, and follow their leader.
2. When this has been reported into the camp of the enemy or into their city, you are able to turn them aside from what they are attempting to do.

3. By doing this you will inspire confidence in your friends, since you are undertaking something and not fearful, and you will prepare fear for your enemies, so that they will keep quiet in their own land.
Chapter 10

1. The following too must be ordered: that those of the citizens who possess teams of animals or slaves deposit them for safekeeping among the neighbouring peoples, as men who will not bring them into the city.

2. And for those who have no friendship with people among whom they may place them, let the magistrates publicly deposit them with the neighbours, arranging the means by which the things deposited will be kept safe.

3. Then make proclamations of the following kind from time to time, for the sake of frightening and deterring the plotters: that men should bring the free persons and the crops into the city, and that, against the man who does not obey, it shall be lawful for anyone who wishes to drive off and carry away, without penalty, what is out in the country.

4. The festivals are to be held within the city, and no private gatherings are to take place anywhere, by day or by night, but necessary ones either in the town-hall or in the council-chamber or in some other public place; and no diviner is to sacrifice privately without the magistrate.

5. Nor are men to dine in common messes, but each in his own house, except at a wedding or a funeral feast, and these having first been announced to the magistrates.
And if there are exiles, proclaim that whoever, of citizens or foreigners or slaves, removes anything, what reward each of these shall have.

6. And if anyone associates with one of the exiles, or with any of their people, or sends or receives letters, let there be some danger or penalty for him. And of letters sent out and brought in, let there be inspection, to whom they are first to be carried.

7. Those who have more than one set of arms are to register them, and no one is to take any weapon out of the city, nor to accept one as a pledge. No one is to hire soldiers, nor to hire himself out, without the magistrates' leave.
8. No citizen or resident alien is to sail out without a token, and the boats are to be ordered beforehand to moor at those gates which will be named in what follows.

9. The foreigners who arrive are to carry their arms in plain sight and ready to hand, and these are to be taken from them at once; and no one is to receive them, nor are the innkeepers to do so, without the magistrates' leave, but the magistrates are to register both who they are and with whom they lodge, whenever they put up.

10. By night the inns are to be closed from outside by the magistrates. And from time to time, all of them who are vagrants are to be proclaimed and expelled. Those of the neighbouring peoples who reside among them for education or some other need are to be registered.

11. With public embassies arriving from cities or tyrants or armies, no one who wishes should be allowed to converse on his own, but there must always be present some of the most trustworthy citizens, who shall remain with them as long as the envoys are in residence.

12. And of whatever the city is short—grain or oil or anything else—let there be set forth, for the man who imports it, interest in proportion to the quantity imported, and let a crown be given him for honour, and to the ship-owner the right of hauling up and launching his ship.

13. Frequent musters under arms are to be held, and the foreigners resident at that time are to withdraw to an appointed place or remain in their houses; and wherever else any of them appears, let a penalty be set as for a wrongdoer.
14. And when the signal is given to these men, the trading-places and shops are to be closed, and the lamps put out, and none of the others is to be still abroad;

15. and whenever some necessity befalls a man, let him go about with a lantern until the contrary order is given. And whoever informs against anyone plotting against the city, or reports any of the aforesaid things being done, let money be announced for him, and let the announced reward be set forth openly in the market-place or on an altar or in a temple, so that one may more readily dare to inform of any of the aforesaid things.

16. Against a monarch or a general or an exile holding power, these things too should be proclaimed beforehand . . . and if the slayer himself should suffer anything, let the announced money be given to his children;

17. and if he have no children, to his nearest kinsman. And if any of those associated with the exile or the monarch or the general does some such deed . . . let what is set forth be given him, and let there be return from exile for him; for through these provisions men would more readily set their hands to it.
18. In a foreign army the following should be done: after calling for silence, let the herald proclaim, all listening,

19. that if anyone wishes to depart, not being content with the present circumstances, he may go away; but afterward . . . he will be sold; and for offences less than these, by the law set forth the penalty is imprisonment. And if anyone is shown to be harming the army, breaking up the camp,

20. let the penalty be death. After this, care must be taken for the rest of the dispositions. And first one must examine whether the citizens are of one mind, since this is the greatest good in a siege; but if not, then of those who hold views opposed to the present order of things . . . and above all, if any have become leaders and authors of some action in the city, one should remove them without arousing suspicion, sending them off elsewhere, on some plausible pretext, as envoys and for other public business.

21. Just so Dionysius dealt with Leptines, his own brother, who stood on familiar terms with the multitude of the Syracusans and whom he saw to be in many ways powerful. Having come into some suspicion of him and wishing to remove him, he did not openly attempt to expel him, knowing that there would be great strength about him, joined with goodwill, and that some revolution might arise; but he contrived as follows.

22. He sent him with a few foreigners to a city named Himera, ordering him to lead out one garrison and install another. And when he was in Himera, Dionysius sent word and ordered him to wait there until he himself should summon him.

23. When a city's children are held hostage, and an expedition is made against it, the parents of the hostages and those near in kin should be removed from the city until the siege is over, that they may not, during the enemy's assaults, behold their own children brought up against the walls along with them and suffering the worst; for it is possible that such men, being within, may do something to the contrary.

24. But if it is difficult to send them out on such pretexts, let them be kept occupied, sharing in as few tasks and operations as possible, and let them have no foreknowledge either of where they will be or of what they will do, and let them be kept least of all by themselves, both night and day; and let the multitude of tasks and services flow over them, one after another, without arousing suspicion, by being engaged in which they will rather be under guard than be guarding anything.

25. Let them be distributed as for surveillance; for, being so disposed, they would least be able to start a revolution.
Furthermore, let no lanterns be carried to their beds, nor any other nocturnal light; for some men, when they are wholly barred from starting any revolution, wishing—though unable to do anything even against the enemy—

26. have devised the following. Carrying lamps, or torches, or lanterns into the watch-posts together with their baskets and bedding, on the pretext of going to rest, they have made a signal by means of these lights; wherefore one must hold all such things suspect.
Chapter 11
1. Furthermore, one must also pay attention to those of the citizens who push counter-purposes, and accept nothing at once, for the following reasons.

2. The plots will be related in order, from the book, by way of example—all those that have occurred in cities at the hands of magistrates or private men, and how some of them, being prevented, came to nothing.

3. For when Chios was about to be betrayed, one of the magistrates, betraying it along with the rest and deceiving his fellow-magistrates, persuaded them by saying that, since there was peace, the harbour-boom should be hauled up onto land and dried and tarred, and the old tackle of the ships sold off, and the leaking parts of the dockyards repaired, and the colonnade adjoining them and the tower in which the magistrates spent their time, adjoining the colonnade—so that, on this pretext, ladders might be provided beforehand for those who intended to seize the dockyards and the colonnade and the tower.
4. Moreover he advised that the multitude of those guarding the city be dismissed from pay, so that the expense to the city might seem as small as possible.

5. And by saying other things of this kind he persuaded his fellow-magistrates to do precisely what was bound to serve the traitors and the attackers toward the capture; so that one must always pay attention to those who are eager to bring such things to completion.

6. At the same time he had tied to the wall and hung down hides of deer and swine, as though wishing to dry them, and elsewhere sails with their ropes outside; by these, in the night, soldiers climbed up.

7. Against political opponents the following was done in Argos. When the rich were about to make a second attempt upon the people and were bringing in foreigners, the leader of the people, learning of what was to come beforehand, made two men, who were among those about to make the attempt and were opposed to the people, his pretended secret friends, and set them up as his enemies, and treated them badly in public, but in silence heard from them the plans of the opposing party.

8. When the rich were in the act of bringing in the foreigners, and at the same time some within the city were ready, and the deed was to take place on the coming night, the leader of the people resolved to summon the assembly with all speed and not to declare beforehand what was coming, that the whole city might not be thrown into confusion; but, saying among other things that it would be expedient that on the coming night all the Argives should be present under arms, each in his own tribe.
9. And if anyone laid out his arms otherwise, or were seen to have carried them elsewhere, let him suffer as a traitor and a plotter against the people.

10. This very thing was so that the rich, being in their tribes, might not be able to gather to one place with the foreigners and make their attempt, but, being in the tribes, might be kept apart, a few among many tribesmen. And this seems to have dissolved the plot well and shrewdly and with safety.

10a. Similarly at Heraclea on the Pontus, when there was a democracy and the rich were plotting against the people and about to make their attempt, the leaders of the people, foreknowing what was to come—there being three tribes among them and four hundred-companies—persuaded the multitude that there should be sixty hundred-companies, so that in these the rich might be distributed for the watches and the other services.
11. And here too it came about that the rich were scattered, and in the hundred-companies few were present at each place among many commons;

12. and something of this kind happened also long ago at Lacedaemon. For when a plot had been disclosed to the magistrates—that when the cap was raised they would make their attempt—they stopped those undertaking to make the attempt by proclaiming that those who intended to raise the cap should not raise it.

13. At Corcyra, when a rising of the rich and oligarchic against the people was to take place (and Chares the Athenian was in residence with a garrison, and he favoured the rising), the following was contrived.

14. Some of the officers of the garrison, after applying cupping-instruments and making cuts on their bodies and getting bloodied, ran out into the market-place as though they had received blows, and at the same time, immediately, the rest of the soldiers, prepared beforehand, brought out their arms, and so did those of the Corcyraeans who were in the plot.

15. While the rest were ignorant of the matter and had been summoned to an assembly, the leaders of the people were seized, on the ground that a rising had come from them, and they reordered the other affairs to their own advantage.
Chapter 12
1. When allies enter the city . . . the allies should never spend their time together, but should be dispersed in the same manner and for the same reasons as set forth above.
2. The same holds when one is about to do something with foreign mercenaries: the citizens who bring them in must always exceed the foreigners in numbers and in power; otherwise,

3. they themselves and the city fall into the foreigners' hands. So when the Chalcedonians were besieged and allies were present . . . the allies of the Chalcedonians sent them a garrison. While the Chalcedonians were deliberating what was expedient for themselves, the garrison-men declared they would not allow it unless it should also seem expedient to the Cyzicenes; so that to the Chalcedonians the garrison within was far more to be feared than the enemy encamped before them.

4. One must therefore never receive into one's own city a greater imported force than the citizens themselves possess; and a city employing foreigners must always far exceed the foreigners' force; for it is not safe to be ruled by foreigners and to come under the power of mercenaries.

5. So it happened to the Heracleots on the Pontus. Bringing in more foreigners than was fitting, they first destroyed their political opponents, then destroyed themselves and the city, being made subject to a tyranny by the man who brought in the foreigners.
Chapter 13

1. If there is need to maintain foreign troops, this would be done most safely as follows. One must order the wealthiest men in the city, each according to his means, to furnish foreigners—some three, some two, some one; and when as many as you need have been gathered, divide them into companies,

2. setting over them the most trustworthy of the citizens as company-commanders. Let the foreigners receive their pay and maintenance from those who hired them, part from them and part from the city contributing.

3. And let them each live in the houses of those who hired them; and let them be gathered for the services and the night-watches and the other duties from the magistrates by the company-commanders who serve them.

4. Let repayment be made, after some time, to those who spend in advance upon the foreigners, deducting the taxes brought into the city by each; for thus foreign troops would be maintained most quickly and most safely and most cheaply.
Chapter 14

1. Toward those in the city who wish to act against the established order, one must bear oneself as has been set forth. But the multitude of the citizens one must, for the time, above all lead toward concord, both by winning them over by other means and by lightening the debtors' burden through a reduction of interest, or by remitting it altogether, and, in cases very perilous, by remitting some part of the debts as well, and all when there is need—since such men are by far the most formidable when in reserve—and by bringing into prosperity those who are in want of the necessities.
2. And how these things might be done fairly and without grieving the rich, and from what resources they might be provided, this too has been written clearly in the book on Resources.
Chapter 15
1. When these arrangements have been made, if anything is reported, or signalled by beacon, as needing relief, one must go out to the parts of the country being harmed.

2. The generals present should immediately form up the men, so that they may not, going out scattered and in small bodies to their own holdings, perish through disorder and untimely exertion, being ambushed by the enemy and suffering harm.

3. But those who come to the gates must gather up to a certain number, say a company or a double company; then, formed up and given a prudent leader, they should so be sent out and hasten on, advancing in formation as much as possible.

4. Then another and another body should be sent out in this way, and quickly, until enough seem to have gone out to the rescue, so that on the march too the divisions may be in contact, and whether one part must aid another, or all must aid at once, it may be easy to join one another and not arrive on the run from far off.

5. Before them the available cavalry and light troops must go out first, and these not in disorder, reconnoitering ahead and seizing beforehand the high ground, so that the hoplites may foreknow the enemy's movements from as far off as possible, and nothing may fall upon them suddenly.

6. At the bends of the ground, and the bases of the hill-tops, and the turnings of the roads, where there are crossroads, there should be signs, so that the men left behind may not be split apart from one another there through ignorance of the way.

7. And in withdrawing to the city one must retire cautiously, for many reasons, and especially fearing an ambush of the enemy; for already something of this kind has happened over an unguarded relief.

8. When the Triballi invaded the territory of the Abderites, the Abderites came out against them and, forming a line, did a most splendid deed; for, engaging, they struck down many and conquered a great and warlike host.

9. But the Triballi, vexed at what had happened, withdrew and recovered themselves, and, coming again into the country and setting ambushes beforehand, ravaged the land of the Abderites not far from the city; and the Abderites, despising them because of their earlier exploit, went out to the rescue in full force with all their strength and zeal; and the Triballi drew them on into the ambushes.

10. Whereupon, it is said, from a single city—of so great a size, indeed—the greatest number perished in the shortest time. For not even on hearing of the destruction of those who had first gone out did the rest hold back from the rescue, but each man, urging on another, hastened to aid those who had gone out, until the city was emptied of men.
Chapter 16
1. The following, then, is another and a better method of relief against those who have invaded.

2. First, then, one must not go to the rescue at once by night, knowing that men would be most disorderly and unprepared before dawn—some hurrying to save their own as quickly as possible from the fields, others fearful of advancing into the dangers, as is natural when things have been freshly announced, and others wholly unprepared.
3. One must, then, ready the relief by gathering it as quickly as possible, at the same time removing the fear from some, inspiring confidence in others, and arming the rest.

4. 5. One must therefore not press upon them and harass them at once, but let them first take courage and, having come to despise you, set out for plunder and gain; and at the same time, glutted with food and drink and made drunk, they would become careless and disobedient to their officers.
6. And from this it is likely that their fights and their withdrawal would go badly for them,

7. provided you set upon them at the right moment. Attack the enemy in circumstances in which you will not have to fight against your will, but, fighting, will not be at a disadvantage against the enemy.

8. 9. But by going to the rescue swiftly, you would endanger your own men, unprepared and not formed up, while the enemy would have done but little harm before you came, and, being still in formation, would go off unpunished.
10. It is much better, as has been written, to give way and attack them when they are off their guard.

12. lay an ambush about the borders (and it is likely that you will get there first, arriving earlier in their country, because they, driving the booty, march more slowly), and make the attack upon them while they are taking their evening meal; for the plunderers, being now in their own land and in safety, turn to relaxation and would be more off their guard.

13. Best of all, so that you may use fresh soldiers, if boats are available, is to make the pursuit by sea; for both getting there first and the rest will fall out for you as needed, provided you are not seen sailing by them.

9. 8. Let these be equal in number to the men gathering, so that, if any are hard pressed, they may climb up quickly; for the gates must not be opened by night, but such ladders must be used, and for anyone else you wish.
